title: Liver Cirrhosis: Diagnosis and Management
subject: Medicine
summary: Liver cirrhosis is the irreversible scarring of the liver, leading to impaired function and portal hypertension. It is a progressive condition with varied causes, often presenting with non-specific symptoms until advanced stages. Early diagnosis and management of underlying causes are crucial to slow progression and prevent life-threatening complications.

sections.p: Liver cirrhosis is a chronic, progressive liver disease characterized by diffuse fibrosis and the formation of regenerative nodules, leading to architectural distortion and impaired liver function. The diagnosis is often suspected clinically and confirmed by imaging and, historically, liver biopsy. In low-resource settings, clinical signs and basic imaging are paramount.
b: Histological confirmation (liver biopsy) remains the gold standard but is often reserved for unclear cases or when specific etiology needs to be determined.
Clinical diagnosis relies on a combination of history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and imaging findings consistent with chronic liver disease and portal hypertension.

sections.p: The severity of liver cirrhosis is assessed using scoring systems that predict prognosis and guide management. These scores help clinicians determine the urgency of intervention and suitability for procedures like liver transplantation.
b: Child-Pugh score: Classifies cirrhosis into A, B, or C based on bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and encephalopathy. Class C indicates severe disease with poor prognosis.

MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score: Used to prioritize patients for liver transplantation, incorporating bilirubin, creatinine, and INR. A higher MELD score indicates more severe disease and higher mortality risk.

sections.p: Identifying the underlying cause of cirrhosis is critical for targeted management and prevention of further damage. In East Africa and similar regions, infectious causes and lifestyle factors are highly prevalent.
b: Chronic viral hepatitis (Hepatitis B and C): Very common causes, especially Hepatitis B in endemic areas.
Alcoholic liver disease: Significant cause globally, including in regions with high alcohol consumption.
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)/Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH): Increasing prevalence due to rising rates of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome.
Schistosomiasis: A parasitic infection common in tropical and subtropical regions, leading to periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension.
Autoimmune hepatitis: Less common but important to consider.
Biliary diseases: Primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Genetic disorders: Hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (less common but important to screen for if suspected).
Drug-induced liver injury: Certain medications or traditional herbal remedies can cause chronic liver damage.

sections.p: Patients with early cirrhosis may be asymptomatic or have non-specific symptoms. As the disease progresses, signs and symptoms of liver dysfunction and portal hypertension become evident.
b: Fatigue, weakness, anorexia, weight loss.
Jaundice: Yellowing of skin and sclera due to impaired bilirubin metabolism.
Ascites: Fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity, often presenting as abdominal distension.
Peripheral edema: Swelling in the legs due to low albumin and increased hydrostatic pressure.
Spider naevi: Small, red, spider-like blood vessels on the skin, especially on the upper body.
Palmar erythema: Reddening of the palms.
Hepatomegaly (early) or shrunken liver (late), splenomegaly (due to portal hypertension).
Encephalopathy: Mental status changes, confusion, asterixis (flapping tremor) due to accumulation of toxins.
Easy bruising or bleeding: Due to impaired synthesis of clotting factors.
Pruritus: Itching, often due to cholestasis.
Dark urine and pale stools: Due to bilirubin excretion abnormalities.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the diagnosis, assess severity, identify the cause, and screen for complications. Availability of tests varies greatly in low-resource settings.

t.b: Screens for anemia (chronic disease, variceal bleeding), thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism), leukopenia. Anemia suggests bleeding or chronic disease. Thrombocytopenia and leukopenia suggest hypersplenism from portal hypertension.

t.a: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) - Bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, Albumin
t.b: Assesses liver synthetic function and hepatocellular damage. Elevated bilirubin indicates impaired excretion. Elevated AST/ALT suggest hepatocellular injury. Low albumin indicates impaired synthetic function. ALP/GGT may suggest cholestasis. Note: AST/ALT may normalize in end-stage cirrhosis despite severe disease.
Measures liver's synthetic function of clotting factors. Prolonged PT/elevated INR indicates impaired synthetic function and increased bleeding risk.

t.a: Renal Function Tests (RFTs) - Creatinine, Urea, Electrolytes
t.b: Screens for renal impairment (hepatorenal syndrome) and electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hyponatremia due to fluid overload/SIADH). Elevated creatinine suggests renal dysfunction. Hyponatremia is common in advanced cirrhosis.

t.a: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), Hepatitis C antibody (anti-HCV)
t.b: Screens for chronic viral hepatitis. Positive results indicate a likely cause of cirrhosis.

Visualizes liver size, texture (nodularity), presence of ascites, splenomegaly, and portal vein patency/flow. Can detect fatty liver, cirrhosis (nodular liver), portal hypertension (splenomegaly, dilated portal vein), and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). If unavailable, clinical signs of portal hypertension and ascites
Tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Elevated levels in a cirrhotic patient raise suspicion for HCC.

Determines the cause of ascites (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, malignancy). Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1 g/dL is highly suggestive of portal hypertension-related ascites. Cell count and culture detect infection.
Screens for esophageal and gastric varices. Essential for risk stratification and primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding.

sections.p: Cirrhosis carries a high risk of life-threatening complications, which often require urgent medical attention. Clinicians must be vigilant for these signs.
b: Variceal bleeding: Sudden, massive hematemesis or melena from ruptured esophageal or gastric varices. This is a medical emergency.
Hepatic encephalopathy: Worsening confusion, disorientation, asterixis, or coma. Can be precipitated by infection, GI bleeding, or electrolyte imbalance.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): Fever, abdominal pain, worsening ascites, or encephalopathy in a patient with ascites. A life-threatening infection.
Hepatorenal syndrome: Progressive renal failure in the absence of other causes of kidney injury, common in advanced cirrhosis.
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC): New onset or worsening abdominal pain, weight loss, or unexplained fever in a cirrhotic patient.
Coagulopathy: Easy bruising, petechiae, or prolonged bleeding from minor trauma due to impaired clotting factor synthesis.
Severe hyponatremia: Can lead to cerebral edema and neurological symptoms.

sections.p: Management of cirrhosis focuses on treating the underlying cause, preventing progression, managing complications, and providing supportive care. In low-resource settings, resourcefulness and prioritization of life-saving interventions are key.
b: Treat the underlying cause:
Antiviral therapy for Hepatitis B or C (if available and indicated).
Abstinence from alcohol for alcoholic liver disease.
Weight management and lifestyle changes for NAFLD/NASH.
Specific treatments for autoimmune or genetic causes.
Management of complications:
Ascites: Sodium restriction, diuretics (spironolactone, furosemide). Paracentesis for large, tense ascites. Avoid NSAIDs.

Variceal bleeding: Endoscopic band ligation or sclerotherapy. Non-selective beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) for primary and secondary prophylaxis. Octreotide to reduce portal pressure acutely. Blood transfusions for significant blood loss.
Hepatic encephalopathy: Lactulose (to reduce ammonia absorption) and rifaximin (to reduce ammonia-producing bacteria in the gut). Identify and treat precipitating factors.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., third-generation cephalosporins like ceftriaxone). Prophylactic antibiotics for high-risk patients.
Hepatorenal syndrome: Volume expansion with albumin, vasoconstrictors (e.g., terlipressin, if available).
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC): Surveillance with ultrasound and AFP. Treatment options vary based on stage and availability (e.g., resection, ablation, transarterial chemoembolization).
General supportive care:
Nutritional support: Adequate protein intake (unless severe encephalopathy), vitamin supplementation.
Avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, paracetamol in high doses).
Vaccinations: Hepatitis A and B, influenza, pneumococcal.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease progression, screen for complications, and adjust management. Prevention focuses on addressing risk factors.
b: Regular clinical assessment for signs of decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, jaundice).
Periodic laboratory tests (LFTs, RFTs, FBC, INR) to monitor liver function and screen for complications.
Ultrasound surveillance every 6 months for HCC in cirrhotic patients.
Endoscopic surveillance for varices as indicated.
Prevention: Hepatitis B vaccination, safe injection practices, responsible alcohol consumption, healthy lifestyle to prevent NAFLD/NASH, early treatment of chronic hepatitis.

sections.p: Several conditions can mimic aspects of liver cirrhosis, making accurate differentiation crucial for appropriate management.
b: Acute liver failure: Rapid onset of severe liver dysfunction in a previously healthy liver, often presenting with encephalopathy and coagulopathy. Cirrhosis is chronic.
Nephrotic syndrome: Can cause severe edema and ascites due to low albumin, but liver function is typically preserved.
Congestive heart failure: Can cause hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema due to fluid overload, but primary liver pathology is absent.
Malignancy with peritoneal carcinomatosis: Can cause ascites, but SAAG is typically low, and imaging may show peritoneal nodules.
Severe malaria: Can cause jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and in severe cases, renal impairment (due to SIADH or acute kidney injury), but is an acute infection.

sections.p: Interpreting laboratory and imaging results in cirrhosis requires clinical context, as some findings can be misleading or appear normal despite significant disease.
b: Normal AST/ALT in advanced cirrhosis: May occur when most hepatocytes are already destroyed, giving a false sense of stable disease.
Preserved renal function: Can be seen in early cirrhosis, but rapid deterioration can occur with precipitating events like infection or dehydration.
Normal alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): Does not rule out HCC, as some tumors do not produce AFP.
Ascitic fluid SAAG <1.1 g/dL: While usually indicating non-portal hypertension causes, can rarely be seen in mixed etiologies or early portal hypertension.
Hyponatremia: Often dilutional due to excess free water retention (SIADH-like state) rather than true sodium depletion, requiring careful fluid management.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe abdominal pain or distension
Vomiting large amounts of blood or passing black, tarry stools
New or worsening confusion, disorientation, or drowsiness
Fever with abdominal pain or worsening ascites
Significant swelling of legs or abdomen that is rapidly worsening
Yellowing of eyes or skin that is rapidly progressing

faq.a: Generally, liver cirrhosis is considered irreversible. However, treating the underlying cause (e.g., viral hepatitis, alcohol abstinence) can halt progression and in some cases, lead to partial regression of fibrosis, improving liver function and prognosis.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of death in cirrhotic patients?
faq.a: The most common causes of death in cirrhotic patients are complications of portal hypertension, particularly variceal bleeding, and infections like spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, followed by hepatocellular carcinoma and hepatorenal syndrome.

faq.q: Why is hyponatremia common in liver cirrhosis?
faq.a: Hyponatremia in cirrhosis is often dilutional, caused by impaired free water excretion due to increased antidiuretic hormone (ADH) activity, leading to water retention that dilutes serum sodium. This is exacerbated by fluid overload and ascites.

exam: A 45-year-old male with known chronic Hepatitis B presents with increasing abdominal distension and confusion. On examination, he has asterixis and shifting dullness. What are your immediate priorities in management? — Secure airway, assess for variceal bleeding (NG tube for blood), rule out SBP (diagnostic paracentesis), administer lactulose for encephalopathy, and consider IV albumin.

You are on a ward round and a patient with cirrhosis develops sudden onset hematemesis. What is the most likely cause and what are your first three steps? — Most likely cause is esophageal variceal bleeding. First steps: secure airway, establish IV access and resuscitate with fluids/blood, administer octreotide, and prepare for urgent endoscopy.

A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops fever and worsening abdominal pain. What is your immediate diagnostic step and why? — Diagnostic paracentesis to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). This is a life-threatening infection requiring urgent diagnosis and empirical antibiotic treatment.

How would you differentiate ascites due to liver cirrhosis from ascites due to peritoneal carcinomatosis in a low-resource setting without advanced imaging? — Clinically, look for other signs of liver disease (jaundice, spider naevi, splenomegaly) in cirrhosis. Ascitic fluid analysis is key: a SAAG >1.1 g/dL strongly suggests portal hypertension (cirrhosis), while a low SAAG suggests other causes like malignancy. Cytology of ascitic fluid can confirm malignancy.

A patient with cirrhosis is prescribed a diuretic for ascites. Which class of diuretic is typically preferred initially and why? — Spironolactone (an aldosterone antagonist) is preferred initially because hyperaldosteronism is common in cirrhosis, contributing to sodium and water retention. It helps counteract this effect and is often combined with furosemide for synergistic action.

Why is it crucial to screen for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in patients with liver cirrhosis, even if they are asymptomatic? — Cirrhosis is the strongest risk factor for HCC. Early detection through regular surveillance (ultrasound and AFP) allows for potentially curative treatments, significantly improving prognosis compared to late-stage diagnosis.

A patient with cirrhosis is found to have a prolonged INR. What is the clinical significance of this finding, and what precautions should be taken? — A prolonged INR indicates impaired liver synthetic function of clotting factors, increasing the risk of bleeding. Precautions include avoiding NSAIDs, careful consideration of invasive procedures, and monitoring for signs of bleeding. Vitamin K supplementation is generally not effective unless there is a true vitamin K deficienc

What are the key differences in managing ascites in cirrhosis versus ascites in nephrotic syndrome? — In cirrhosis, ascites is due to portal hypertension and low albumin, managed with sodium restriction and diuretics (spironolactone, furosemide). In nephrotic syndrome, ascites is primarily due to severe hypoalbuminemia from protein loss in urine, managed with protein replacement, diuretics, and treating the underlying kidney disease. Fluid restriction is often more stringent
